sources.locator: Chapter I §5 Example 25, printed pp. 91–93; §5 (5.1)–(5.12) and (5.16)–(5.17), printed pp. 69–74; §7 (7.1)–(7.6), printed pp. 112–116, Example 3, printed pp. 116–117, and Example 26, printed p. 134; §9 (9.1)–(9.7), printed pp. 142–148

contents.name: I §5 Example 25: the diagonal map (Δf)(x,y)=f(x,y), the counit and the cocommutative Hopf algebra structure on Λ, with Δh_n=Σ_{p+q=n}h_p⊗h_q and Δe_n=Σ_{p+q=n}e_p⊗e_q
I §7 (7.1)–(7.3): the ring R=⊕_n R(S_n) with the outer induction product, and the proof that the characteristic map is an isometric ring isomorphism onto Λ
I §7 Example 26: the comultiplication δf=Σ_{p+q=n} f↓_{S_p×S_q} on R corresponding to Λ→Λ⊗Λ under the characteristic map
I §9 (9.1)–(9.3): the definition of c^λ_{μν} as the coefficient of s_λ in s_μs_ν, the identity s_{λ/μ}=Σ_ν c^λ_{μν}s_ν, and |Tab(λ−μ,π)|=⟨s_{λ/μ},h_π⟩

I §9 (9.4)–(9.7): the Littlewood–Robinson bijection, the substitution S_{r−1,r} on the first maximal bad r-index, its reversibility (9.5), tableau compatibility preservation (9.6) and the decreasing-row lemma (9.7)
I §5 (5.1)–(5.12): skew Schur functions by Hall adjointness, the skew Jacobi–Trudi identity and the skew tableau expansion
I §5 (5.16)–(5.17): the Pieri rules s_μh_r and s_μe_r over horizontal and vertical strips
I §7 Example 3: the characteristic of a skew character, and restriction of χ^λ to S_m×S_n governed by skew Schur functions
I §7 Examples 20 and 23: the internal (Kronecker) product s_λ*s_μ and its diagonalisation on power sums
contents.reason: The internal product and Kronecker coefficients are the topic of the later planned page kronecker-coefficients-and-internal-products (SYMR-13); no item of this pair asserts an internal-product rule.

contents.name: Appendix A §6: the polynomial-functor construction of the outer induction product over GL_r
contents.reason: This pair proves only the symmetric-group outer product and its translation to symmetric functions; the polynomial-functor and GL_r tensor-product machinery is owned by tensor-product-multiplicities-and-littlewood-richardson and is neither re-derived nor claimed here.

contents.name: I §7 Example 3: the restriction character on S_m×S_r and its skew-character coefficients; the local item identifies those coefficients with the explicit S_m-intertwiner module and proves its S_r Specht decomposition.
I §5 (5.16): the horizontal-strip Pieri rule specialized to multiplying S^(3,2) by the trivial S_2 factor; the local example enumerates every size-7 shape and checks its two added columns.

I §7 Examples 3 and 26: compute the five restriction-coproduct bidegrees of χ^(3,1) for S_4 from every subshape of (3,1), explicitly count the small LR tableaux, and check that each component has identity value 3

sources.title: Darij Grinberg and Victor Reiner, Hopf Algebras in Combinatorics (complete author-hosted lecture-notes book, 2020)

contents.name: §1.2–1.3: definitions of coalgebras and bialgebras (coassociativity, counit, compatibility of product and coproduct) and of bialgebra morphisms
§1.4: the convolution algebra Hom(A,A), antipodes and Hopf algebras; Proposition 1.4.14 (tensor products of Hopf algebras)

§1.4, Proposition 1.4.16: a connected graded bialgebra has a unique antipode, defined recursively on homogeneous components by a left ⋆-inverse and identified with a right ⋆-inverse by associativity of the convolution product
§2.3, Proposition 2.3.6: the comultiplication on Λ as the two-alphabet diagonal map, with Δh_n=Σ_{p+q=n}h_p⊗h_q and Δs_{λ/ν} expanded over intermediate partitions
§2.4, Proposition 2.4.1 and Definition 2.4.2: the fundamental involution ω with ω(e_n)=h_n, and the antipode of Λ with S(e_n)=(−1)^n h_n and S(h_n)=(−1)^n e_n

§4.2–4.3, Definitions 4.2.1–4.3.4, bialgebra compatibility (4.3.1), and Proposition 4.3.7(a): the induction-restriction identity and Young-subgroup double cosets; the source leaves intersection bookkeeping to the reader, supplied explicitly in the item proof.
§4.1, Theorem 4.1.7: Mackey’s restriction-after-induction formula for finite groups, used with the explicitly constructed matrix-indexed representatives from §4.3.

contents.name: §14 Example 14.5: the explicit computation [3,2][2]=[5,2]+[4,3]+[4,2,1]+[3,3,1]+[3,2,2] from Young's rule
§16 Theorem 16.4: the Littlewood–Richardson rule [λ][μ]=Σ_ν c^λ_{μν}[ν] for the outer product of Specht modules
§14 Example 14.4 and the Young's-rule method: the product [m][n] expanded by horizontal strips, and the reduction of a product of two Specht modules to Young's rule
§16 Lemmas 16.1–16.3: the operators A_c and R_c and the leading-configuration lemma used in James's operator proof of Theorem 16.4
contents.reason: This pair proves the Littlewood–Richardson rule by the Littlewood–Robinson bijection of Macdonald I §9, not by James's A_c/R_c operator argument; his Lemma 16.3 and its notation are neither needed nor restated, so no item carries them.
